newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Basic says Guatemala crude loss not dire.
newsitem.headline: Basic says Guatemala crude loss not dire.

text.p: Five days of lost production while protestors occupied Guatemala's only refinery did not have a significant impact on crude exports, Guatemala's oil company said on Tuesday.

The refinery processes 2,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude to produce asphalt for national consumption and for export within Central America. It exports the remainder, about 21,000 bpd of crude of a total 23,000 bpd produced.
"It doesn't dramatically affect us," spokesman for Basic Resources International Ltd. Luis de Leon told Reuters, referring to the halt in output.

De Leon said crude oil extracted by Basic is only exported by tanker two times a month. He said there was not an immediate effect on orders or buyers even though production was completely halted for five consecutive days.
"What has not been produced are some 100,000 barrels of (crude) oil and some 10,000 barrels of asphalt," de Leon said.
De Leon said Basic would have to pay for space in the tanker even if it is not filled completely when it arrives at the end of the month.

Basic's refinery in the northern Peten region was forced shut for five days as some 300 protestors occupied the refinery to demand back pay for helping the government fight rebels. The army forcefully removed the protestors on Tuesday.
De Leon said production at all of Basic's wells in the Xan oil field in Peten was suspended during the occupation.
Most of Basic's crude is not processed in the refinery, but it all passes through the refinery en route to the Caribbean coast.
Employees planned to return to Basic's refinery late Tuesday and operations could return to normal by Wednesday, De Leon said.
Army and police forces removed the protestors Tuesday morning without incident. It was the third time this year the same protestors have forced a shut down at the plant.
Deputy Interior Minister Salvador Gandara told reporters on Tuesday that the government may put a permanent military installation near the refinery to deter further protests.
Basic, which was recently purchased by Canada's Norcen Energy Resources LTD, has operated in Guatemala for 20 years and has taken regular disturbances here in stride.
During the 1980s, leftist rebels regularly attacked and sabotaged Basic operations, including blowing up pipelines.

Aside from two previous occupations of the refinery this year, Basic slowed exports for two weeks in November 1996 when truckers went on strike to protest the imminent loss of their jobs when Basic completed its pipeline in December.
